papers.title: Speculative Decoding for Semantic-ID-Based Generative Recommendations
papers.abstract: Generative recommender systems with Semantic IDs (SIDs) represent each item as a short sequence of $L$ discrete tokens and use a sequence model to predict the next item's tokens from a user's history. Industry-scale deployments typically use these models to retrieve multiple candidates per request with constrained beam search. However, this incurs a fixed cost of $L$ sequential model calls per request, and accuracy degrades as the SID generator becomes less sharp, without a guarantee on how close the output is to the exact top-$K$. Production systems therefore cannot detect degraded retrieval for individual requests. We propose SIDECAR, which uses approximate draft candidates and a tree-attention pass to score the entire draft in a single model call, memory permitting. This pass bounds the probability of every unexplored SID prefix and certifies the exact top-$K$ if the draft contains them. Otherwise, a branch-and-bound fallback expands only the parts of the trie that can still change the output, reaching certification within at most $L$ calls for any draft. Moreover, under a budget of $M$ tokens per call and $Y$ calls, which for $Y = L$ matches the resources of a beam search of width $M$, SIDECAR announces a factor $1 + \delta$ within which its list will be exact at every rank. Depending on model sharpness, SIDECAR returns the exact top-$K$ using a fraction of beam search's calls or memory. Even when the budget is too small to recover the exact top-$K$, SIDECAR, unlike beam search, reports the announced factor, allowing the serving system to stop early once a quality target or latency limit is reached.
papers.summary: Generative recommenders that use Semantic IDs represent each item as a short sequence of discrete tokens and usually retrieve several candidates with constrained beam search. That design pays a fixed sequence of model calls on every request. As the generator becomes less sharp, the list can drift from the exact top-K, and the serving system cannot tell when a single request has degraded. SIDECAR first scores an approximate draft with one tree-attention pass and places probability bounds on unexplored prefixes, so it can certify the exact top-K when the draft already contains it. Otherwise it expands only the branches that can still change the output. With a user-sequence draft that contains one interaction, the median request finishes in about 1.7 calls, and about 40% of requests are certified on the first pass. Even when the budget is too small to recover the exact list, it reports a factor around the true ranking, so serving can stop once a quality or latency limit is reached.

papers.title: Towards Realistic Evaluation of Uncertainty Quantification for LLM-Based Recommender Systems
papers.authors: Hao Wu, Sipeng Chen, Weikai Li, Tianyi Chen, Qiancheng Yang, Hang Zhou, Yizhou Sun, Wei Wang, Xiao Luo
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) provide a flexible interface for recommendation systems. However, their issued rankings require reliable instance-level uncertainty monitoring. In this scenario, comparing uncertainty quantification (UQ) methods becomes challenging because LLM rankers lack a standard item-classification head. Their scores may depend on option labels, prompts, generation procedures, and the available user and item evidence. Existing methods derive uncertainty from different sources and apply it at different stages of the recommendation process. Some methods evaluate an issued ranking, whereas others use uncertainty to change the ranking itself, making direct comparison difficult. Here we introduce a fixed-ranking benchmark which evaluates eight heterogeneous UQ signals as record-level monitors under a shared output contract. We evaluate these signals across four recommendation datasets and two LLM backbones under a shared fixed-ranking protocol. From the results, we draw three main observations. First, UQ method ordering changes across backbones even on the same reference instances. Second, ranking-aligned Top10Mass provides the strongest scalar Error@10 detection in several evaluation conditions, reflecting effective cutoff-aligned monitoring, while its advantage narrows for popularity-tail targets. Third, scalar UQ signals are weak at identifying which control has the larger clipped NDCG@10 difference, whereas source-specific signals, including Perturbation Rank Instability and simple listwise distances, provide stronger paired-control agreement, reflecting their sensitivity to the two controlled evidence sources. These findings motivate us to evaluate ranking-failure detection, robustness across recommendation conditions, and responses to controlled evidence changes as distinct properties of UQ.
papers.summary: When large language models rank items, each request needs a reliable uncertainty monitor, but existing methods draw signals from different sources and apply them at different stages. Some only score an issued ranking, while others use uncertainty to change the ranking itself, so comparisons can mix monitoring quality with reranking effects. A new fixed-ranking benchmark evaluates eight heterogeneous uncertainty signals as record-level monitors under one output contract, across four recommendation datasets and two LLM backbones. Method orderings change with the backbone. Ranking-aligned Top10Mass gives the strongest Error@10 detection under several Llama conditions, but the advantage is uneven: overall AUROC is 0.634 under sparse history and falls to 0.547 on the popularity-tail subset. Scalar signals are also weak at telling whether user history or item text had the larger effect.

papers.title: LazUnirec: Unifying Retrieval and Ranking in Multi-scenario Industrial Recommendation
papers.authors: Xiaodong Li, Junfeng Zhang, Shichao Nie, Ziyue Guo, Yiming Liu, Xinxin Xu, Xurong Li, Jinyuan Dang, Zhanming Ou, Jianan Yan, Tao Luo, Xiaoyi Zeng
papers.abstract: Modern industrial recommendation systems typically divide retrieval and ranking into two separate cascaded stages, leading to inconsistent optimization objectives, redundant encoding of user sequences, and a waste of computational resources. Previous efforts have investigated using Transformers to model both retrieval and ranking simultaneously. However, these studies still face two major limitations: (1) Since retrieval and ranking share a single Transformer backbone, the gradient conflict arises when the gradient directions of the two tasks are inconsistent. (2) When gradient conflict occurs, the model cannot determine a reliable direction for gradient updates. To this end, we propose a Unified Retrieval and Ranking approach for Multi-scenario Industrial Recommendation, termed as LazUnirec. Specifically, we construct task-shared and task-private parameters on the Transformer backbone to mitigate the gradient conflict. Wherein, for the attention components, we propose LoRA-modulated attention, enabling retrieval and ranking to share attention parameters while preserving task-private parameters. For the feed-forward networks (FFN), we present task-adaptive sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) to mitigate gradient conflict by constructing task-shared and task-private experts. Moreover, we propose an uncertainty estimation that evaluates the gradient reliability of the retrieval and ranking, thereby guiding the model toward a more reliable gradient update direction when gradient conflict occurs. In addition, knowledge distillation from ranking to retrieval further enables cross-task knowledge transfer. Extensive offline experiments and online A/B testing demonstrate the effectiveness and superiority of LazUnirec. LazUnirec has been deployed in online multi-scenario industrial recommendation system and currently delivers significant gains for the platform.
papers.summary: Industrial recommenders usually cascade retrieval and ranking as two stages, so their objectives diverge and the user sequence is encoded twice. If the two tasks share one Transformer, conflicting gradients show up in both attention and feed-forward layers, and the model is left without a reliable update direction. LazUnirec keeps both shared and task-private parameters on one backbone, using LoRA-modulated attention and a task-adaptive sparse MoE in the feed-forward layers. When gradients conflict, it uses uncertainty estimates to choose a more reliable direction, then distills knowledge from ranking into retrieval so the two tasks can help each other. Alibaba International Digital Commerce Group has already deployed it in a multi-scenario industrial recommender. An online A/B test ran for one week on ten percent of traffic. In trigger-free scenarios, item page views rose 5.25% and GMV rose 4.01%; in trigger-based scenarios, GMV rose 3.06%.

papers.title: C3H: Compression-to-Consensus Criteria Hijacking in Multimodal LLM Recommender Systems
papers.authors: Guowei Guan, Yurong Hao, Jiaming Zhang, Fuyao Zhang, Wei Yang Bryan Lim
papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are transforming recommender systems into content-aware decision systems. In these systems, multimodal compression and cross-modal fusion are often viewed as robustness-enhancing mechanisms against content manipulation, as compression can filter noisy signals and cross-modal consensus can suppress inconsistent anomalies. We challenge this assumption by showing that the same process can expose a compression-to-consensus (C2C) bias in ranking decisions. Signals that remain salient after compression and receive consistent support across modalities can gain disproportionate influence in candidate comparison, offering an exploitable direction for content manipulation. In this paper, we introduce C3H, a novel inference-time attack that exploits this vulnerability. Rather than relying on noisy perturbations or training-time poisoning, C3H promotes a target item by tailoring its multimodal content to align with the decision criteria implicitly expressed by the recommender. Extensive experiments demonstrate that C3H substantially increases target-item exposure while maintaining overall recommendation utility. Code is available at this https URL.
papers.summary: Multimodal LLM recommenders often treat compression and cross-modal fusion as defenses, on the view that compression filters noise and agreement across modalities suppresses anomalies. The same process can also give outsized rank influence to cues that stay salient after compression and are reinforced across modalities, which opens a path for content manipulation. C3H does not query the victim model or poison training. It rewrites a target item's text and image to match the decision criteria the recommender already implies. On VIP5, its ER@20 reaches 1.1 times to 1.8 times the next-best method in every dataset and prompt setting. The same content, transferred unchanged to Qwen2-VL-2B-Instruct, leads by 4.7 times on Sports at the high end. Three anomaly-based content filters barely work: exposure shifts by less than 0.004, while utility for ordinary users stays largely intact.

scenario: Today's generative-recommendation papers split between certifying Semantic-ID lists, comparing uncertainty monitors fairly, unifying industrial retrieval and ranking, and showing that multimodal compression can itself be used to buy exposure. Some decoders can prove that the current list is the exact top-K, or else report a factor when the budget is too tight. Some evaluations hold the ranking fixed and compare only monitoring signals, so reranking effects are not counted as better uncertainty estimates. A unified online model has already raised platform GMV, while the attack work shows that cues which survive compression and are reinforced across modalities can become a query-free lever for manipulation.
